newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to cement relationship with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Spain to cement relationship with NATO.

text.p: Spain will cement its relationship with NATO this week when parliament is expected to endorse full integration into the alliance's military command.
A two-day debate on the government resolution began on Wednesday with broad support highlighting Spain's efforts to tie itself more closely to Europe and the United States.
The text of the resolution, published on Wednesday by Spanish news agency EFE, said full integration in a "reformed" NATO will serve Spain's political and security interests.
"Since 1990, the Atlantic alliance has experienced a profound process of transformation to adapt its political and military structures to the new geo-strategic environment," the resolution said.
Conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government has the backing of opposition Socialist party leader Felipe Gonzalez, virtually assuring the resolution's passage in a vote set for Thursday.

Spain, under former Prime Minister Gonzalez, joined NATO in 1982 but froze integration into the military wing pending a referendum on continued membership. The 1986 referendum passed with 52 percent of voters saying "yes".
But Spaniards' support came with a few strings attached.

The government promised in return a reduction in U.S. troops stationed in Spain which then numbered 12,500. The country was to remain free of nuclear weapons. And Gonzalez vowed Spain would stay outside NATO's military command structure.

Aznar, who took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule, says circumstances have been transformed beyond recognition by the end of the Cold War and by the alliance's decision this year to allow European allies to use NATO equipment and resources for their own operations.
With the resolution, the government will demand it host the NATO command controlling all of the Iberian peninsula including access to the Mediterranean through the Straits of Gibraltar.
It will also stipulate that Spain remain free of nuclear weapons.
In 1986, the government saw its relationship with NATO as the key to closer ties with western Europe at a time Spain was trying to shed decades of isolation.
The referendum came just three months after Spain had joined the European Community and Gonzalez said then the country could not shirk its responsibilities for European defence.
He also warned Spain would suffer dire economic consequences if it turned its back on countries with which it did 75 percent of its trade.

This time around, the deepening of ties with NATO takes place against the backdrop of Spanish efforts to discipline its economy so it can qualify for the founding group of states in a European economic and monetary union in 1999.
Spain will take on its new role in NATO at a time when the organisation is looking to cast its net wider to include former Soviet bloc members, an expansion firmly supported by Spain.
Aznar's government has fostered warm ties with the United States and has pleased Washington by taking a tougher stance on Cuba than his predecessor.
The main holdout in parliament against full intergration is parliament is Julio Anguita's pacifistic United Left communist party.

Traditional opposition in Spain to joining NATO's military structure came from a coalition of trade unions, pacifists, artists, ecologists and far left groups who feared nuclear war and were hostile to the United States for its support of the late Spanish dictator General Francisco Franco.
